newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- possible calm after the storm.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- possible calm after the storm.

text.p: U.S. credit markets are expected to stabilize a bit on Thursday after Wednesday's mammoth selloff following hawkish remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, economists said.
But they added the overall market trend is still bearish and a further backup in yields can be expected.

"We could see considerably more downside (in prices) ... with the long bond yield going backup to 6.95 and 6.96 percent," said Lee Youngdahl, economist and vice president at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 1-19/32 at 98-00 in late Wednesday trade. Its yield jumped sharply to 6.78 percent from 6.66 percent on Tuesday.
Analysts said the market turned mostly bearish after the first leg of Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday.
The Fed chairman said he sees upside inflation risks, adding that he could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening of monetary policy.
"What (Greenspan's remarks) do to people's minds is that it moves up the timetable," Youngdahl said.

"While the market was sort of pushing tightening further and further out into the future, Greenspan turned that around again to where something is probably likely to occur by the spring time," the economist added.

Analysts said, however, the dollar's strong performance against other major currencies on Wednesday hinted that foreign investors do not appear to be ready to bail out of the U.S. Treasury market yet.
"The dollar has been very strong today," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards and Sons Inc.
"It seems to me foreign investors are focusing more on the idea that the economic conditions are still pretty good, that is strong growth with low inflation," Thayer added.

Some analysts said they believe the market might have some room to recover over the next few weeks, mainly after the deluge of fresh Treasury supply, which included a quarterly refunding and two- and five-year note sales, is mostly over.

"It might be that we've just got a temporary reaction to (Greenspan's) comments ... and over the next couple of weeks, particularly now that the Treasury auctions are out of the way, we might see prices recover a bit," Thayer said.
Despite Greenspan's warning comments, analysts said the economy is far from reaching a point of overheating.
"The economy is still running hot, but we don't have an overheating situation as of yet," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
On the economic data front on Thursday, the market will take in the January durable goods report at 0830 EST/1330 GMT as well as jobless claims for the week ended February 22.
Also, players will learn about the New York NAPM index for February, the APICS survey for February and the January help wanted index.
On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve added temporary reserves to the banking system through eight-day fixed system repurchase agreements, when the federal funds were traded at 5-7/16 percent.
Fed funds are seen opening at 5.31 percent on Thursday, above the central bank's 5.25 percent target for the rate.
